name: Backend & Software Foundations
role: The software craft every AI role stands on: Python and TypeScript, data structures, Git and Linux, debugging, API styles, PostgreSQL and document stores, identity (OAuth2, OIDC, SAML, RBAC/ABAC), caching and queues, webhooks, API design and resilience. Day to day: build and harden the services, integrations and data paths that agents call.

subjects.title: Python and TypeScript for AI Engineers
subjects.why: Almost every agent, connector and eval harness is Python or TypeScript. Typed, async, validated code is the difference between a demo and a service.
subjects.explainer:
AI engineers live in two languages. Python owns models, data and evals. TypeScript owns product front-ends, edge functions and many agent SDKs. You don't need every corner of either, but you do need the same production habits in both: type hints, schema validation at every boundary, async I/O for slow network calls, packaging that reproduces, and tests.

The common failure isn't syntax. It's untyped dictionaries flowing from an LLM into business logic, blocking calls inside an event loop, and 'works on my laptop' environments.

resources.title: The Python Tutorial (official)
resources.why: The official tutorial, aimed at programmers new to Python. Covers data structures, modules, errors, classes and the standard library tour in an afternoon.

resources.title: TypeScript Handbook
resources.why: The official handbook: everyday types, narrowing, generics, object types and modules. Read 'The Basics' and 'Everyday Types' first.

resources.title: Pydantic documentation
resources.why: Models, fields, validators, JSON Schema generation, strict mode and serialization. The validation layer used by FastAPI and most LLM SDKs.

resources.title: FastAPI documentation
resources.why: Typed Python web APIs with automatic validation and OpenAPI docs. Its tutorial covers path/query parameters, request bodies, dependencies and async.

resources.title: mypy documentation
resources.why: The type-hints cheat sheet, how to adopt mypy in an existing codebase, protocols and structural subtyping.

resources.title: Dropbox: Our journey to type checking 4 million lines of Python
resources.why: Jukka Lehtosalo's 2019 account of how Dropbox adopted mypy incrementally, including the performance work and the case for types as verified documentation.

subjects.project: Build a typed FastAPI service with a Pydantic request/response model that calls an LLM asynchronously, plus a small TypeScript client generated from its OpenAPI schema.

topics.title: Production Python
topics.explainer: Production Python for AI work means four habits. First, type hints everywhere, checked by mypy or pyright, so refactors are safe. Second, Pydantic models at every boundary (HTTP input, LLM output, tool arguments), so bad data fails loudly and early. Third, asyncio for network-bound work: an agent mostly waits on model and API calls, so concurrency matters more than raw speed. Fourth, reproducible environments with a lockfile (uv, Poetry or pip-tools) and pinned model SDK versions, because SDKs change quickly.

subtopics.title: Type hints and mypy
subtopics.text: Annotate functions and run a type checker in CI; it catches None-handling and wrong-argument bugs before production.

subtopics.title: Pydantic validation
subtopics.text: Parse, don't trust: turn raw JSON from users, tools and LLMs into validated models with clear errors.

subtopics.title: asyncio and concurrency
subtopics.text: Use async clients and asyncio.gather for parallel model and API calls; never block the event loop with sync I/O.

subtopics.title: Packaging and environments
subtopics.text: Lock dependencies, pin SDK versions and build the same container locally and in CI.

topics.title: TypeScript for AI products
topics.explainer: TypeScript matters because the product surface (web apps, browser extensions, edge functions, many MCP servers and agent SDKs) is written in it. Its value is static types over JavaScript's flexibility: you describe the shape of an API response once and the compiler checks every use. Pair it with a runtime validator such as Zod, because TypeScript types vanish at runtime and LLM output is untrusted. Learn promises and async/await, streaming with fetch and ReadableStream, and how to generate types from an OpenAPI or JSON schema so client and server never drift.

subtopics.title: Static types vs runtime validation
subtopics.text: Types check your code at compile time; a runtime schema (Zod) checks the data you actually receive.

subtopics.title: async/await and streaming
subtopics.text: Stream tokens to the UI with fetch and ReadableStream or server-sent events instead of waiting for the full answer.

subtopics.title: Generated clients
subtopics.text: Generate TypeScript types from the server's OpenAPI document so contract changes break the build, not production.

subtopics.title: Node, Deno, Bun and edge runtimes
subtopics.text: Know which runtime your code runs on; edge runtimes restrict APIs such as the filesystem and long-running work.

quiz.q: An LLM returns JSON for a tool call. What is the safest first step in Python?
choices: Validate it into a Pydantic model and handle validation errors
Pass the dict straight to the function
Assume the schema is followed because you asked nicely
quiz.why: Model output is untrusted input; validate before use and feed errors back.

quiz.q: Why use asyncio in an agent service?
choices: Most time is spent waiting on network calls, so concurrency raises throughput
It removes the need for timeouts
quiz.why: Agents are I/O-bound; async lets one process overlap many waits.

quiz.q: TypeScript types protect you from bad API data at runtime.
choices: False: types are erased; you need runtime validation such as Zod
True, but only in strict mode
False, because TypeScript has no types
quiz.why: Static types disappear after compilation; validate untrusted data at runtime.

lesson.intuition: Think of types and schemas as the contracts between the pieces of an AI system. A model, a tool, a database and a UI all speak in JSON, and JSON lies easily: a missing field, a string where a number should be, a null nobody expected. Typed Python and TypeScript, plus runtime validation at each boundary, turn those silent lies into loud, early, fixable errors.
how: Define the data shapes once (Pydantic models in Python, Zod schemas or generated types in TypeScript).
Validate every boundary: HTTP input, LLM output, tool arguments and third-party API responses.
Make network-bound work async and give every call a timeout.
Run a type checker and tests in CI on every change.
Lock dependencies and pin model SDK versions so builds reproduce.
lesson.example: An agent asks a model for {"order_id": "A-17", "refund_usd": 20}. One day the model returns refund_usd as "twenty". Without validation, the string reaches the payment code and crashes, or worse, is coerced. With a Pydantic model (order_id: str, refund_usd: float with gt=0, le=500), validation fails, the error text goes back to the model, and the retry returns 20.0. The cap at 500 also blocks an injected request for 5,000.
mistakes: Passing raw dicts from the model straight into business logic.
Calling a synchronous HTTP client inside an async handler, which freezes every other request.
Trusting TypeScript types for runtime data instead of validating it.
Unpinned SDK versions that change behaviour between deploys.
lesson.enterprise: A support team's FastAPI service calls three tools per request. Moving the calls from sequential requests to asyncio.gather, with a 10-second timeout each, cuts p95 latency from about 9 s to 4 s. Adding Pydantic models for tool outputs turns a weekly production crash into a logged validation error.
takeaways: Validate every boundary; LLM output is untrusted input.
Agents are I/O-bound: async plus timeouts beats faster code.
Types plus a checker in CI make large codebases refactorable.
Generate clients from schemas so front end and back end never drift.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U["User / UI (TypeScript)"] -->|"typed request"| API["FastAPI (Pydantic in)"]
  API -->|"async + timeout"| LLM["LLM"]
  LLM -->|"raw JSON"| V{"Validate (Pydantic)"}
  V -->|"ok"| BL["Business logic"]
  V -->|"error text"| LLM
  BL --> OUT["Typed response (OpenAPI)"]
  OUT --> U
lesson.diagramAlt: A typed request flows from a TypeScript UI to a FastAPI service, which calls an LLM asynchronously. The model's raw JSON is validated; failures go back to the model, and valid data reaches business logic and returns as a typed response.

case.title: Our journey to type checking 4 million lines of Python (Dropbox Tech, 2019)
case.summary: Dropbox, a heavy Python user, adopted static type checking with mypy and grew coverage to 4 million lines of annotated code. The post explains why: type annotations act as verified documentation, and a type checker finds subtle bugs such as forgetting to handle None. It also describes the performance work needed to keep mypy fast at that scale.
case.lesson: Adopt types incrementally and invest in tooling speed. At scale, being able to understand code becomes the main constraint on productivity.

subjects.title: Data Structures and Algorithms That Matter in Practice
subjects.why: You won't hand-roll red-black trees, but choosing a dict over a list scan, a heap over a sort, or a linear regex over a backtracking one decides whether a system holds up.
subjects.explainer:
Practical DSA for AI engineers is about recognizing complexity in everyday code: hash maps for lookups, sets for dedup, heaps for top-k, queues for BFS and work scheduling, sorting plus binary search, and graphs for dependencies and lineage. Big-O matters when n is a million chunks, a hundred thousand tickets, or an attacker-controlled string.

Learn the standard-library tools first: dict, set, collections.deque, heapq and bisect in Python. Know the cost of each operation, and treat any nested loop over large inputs as a review flag.

resources.title: Python wiki: TimeComplexity
resources.why: Archived python.org page listing the big-O cost of operations on list, deque, set and dict in CPython. Keep it open when choosing containers.

resources.title: heapq: heap queue algorithm (Python docs)
resources.why: The standard-library priority queue: heappush/heappop, nlargest/nsmallest and merge, with notes on stability and priority-queue implementation.

resources.title: USF Data Structure Visualizations
resources.why: Animated visualizations of stacks, queues, hash tables, heaps, trees, sorting and graph algorithms. Step through each operation to build intuition.

resources.title: Coding Interview University
resources.why: A complete self-study computer science plan (complexity, data structures, sorting, graphs, recursion) with curated videos. Use it as a checklist, not a mandate.

resources.title: Cloudflare: Details of the outage on July 2, 2019
resources.why: Cloudflare's post-mortem: one WAF rule's regex backtracked enormously, exhausting CPU worldwide for 27 minutes. It includes a readable explanation of regex backtracking.

subjects.project: Profile a slow dedup-and-rank step in a RAG pipeline, replace list scans with sets and a full sort with heapq.nlargest, and report the before/after timings.

topics.title: Core structures and their costs
topics.explainer: Most performance bugs come from the wrong container. A Python list membership test scans every element (O(n)); a set or dict lookup is O(1) on average. Appending to a list is cheap, but inserting at the front is O(n); collections.deque fixes that for queues. When you need the best k of n items, a heap gives O(n log k) instead of sorting everything. When data is sorted, bisect finds positions in O(log n). Write down the operation you do most often, then pick the structure that makes it cheap.

subtopics.title: Hash maps and sets
subtopics.text: Use them for membership, counting and joins in memory; average O(1) lookups.

subtopics.title: Queues and deques
subtopics.text: Use deque for FIFO work queues and BFS; popleft is O(1), list.pop(0) is O(n).

subtopics.title: Heaps for top-k
subtopics.text: heapq.nlargest(k, items) keeps only k candidates, ideal for reranking or scheduling.

subtopics.title: Sorting and binary search
subtopics.text: Sort once (O(n log n)), then answer many range or position queries with bisect in O(log n).

topics.title: Graphs, recursion and complexity traps
topics.explainer: Graphs model a lot of AI systems: agent plans as task DAGs, data lineage, service dependencies and permission hierarchies. Topological sort orders a DAG of tasks, BFS finds shortest hops, and cycle detection catches circular dependencies. Complexity traps hide in innocent code: a nested loop comparing every pair of 100,000 chunks is 10 billion comparisons, recursion without memoization can explode exponentially, and some regular expressions backtrack exponentially on hostile input. Recognize the pattern, estimate n, and measure before and after.

subtopics.title: Topological sort
subtopics.text: Order tasks so every dependency runs first; use it for pipelines and multi-step agent plans.

subtopics.title: BFS and DFS
subtopics.text: Traverse dependency or lineage graphs; BFS gives the shortest path in hops.

subtopics.title: Memoization
subtopics.text: Cache results of pure recursive calls (functools.lru_cache) to avoid recomputing subproblems.

subtopics.title: Regex backtracking
subtopics.text: Nested quantifiers like (a+)+ can take exponential time; prefer linear-time engines such as RE2 for untrusted input.

quiz.q: You dedupe 1M chunk hashes with `if h not in seen_list`. What is the fix?
choices: Use a set, turning O(n²) total work into about O(n)
Sort the list after every insert
quiz.why: List membership is O(n); set membership is O(1) on average.

quiz.q: Best way to get the top 10 of 5 million scored candidates?
quiz.why: A heap of size k costs O(n log k) and little memory.

quiz.q: Why can a single regular expression take down a service?
choices: Backtracking engines can take exponential time on some inputs
Regex is O(1) but uses too much memory
quiz.why: Catastrophic backtracking is an algorithmic-complexity bug; Cloudflare's 2019 outage is the classic example.

lesson.intuition: Data structures are about making the operation you do most often cheap. If you mostly ask 'have I seen this?', you want a set. If you mostly ask 'what's the best item right now?', you want a heap. If you mostly ask 'what must happen first?', you want a graph and a topological sort. Algorithms only feel academic until n gets big, or until an attacker picks n for you.
how: Name the dominant operation (lookup, top-k, ordering, traversal).
Pick the container that makes it cheap (dict/set, heap, deque, sorted list plus bisect, graph).
Estimate n in production, not in your test fixture.
Measure with timeit or a profiler before and after.
Guard untrusted input with linear-time algorithms and size limits.
lesson.example: A RAG pipeline dedupes 200,000 chunks by checking `if h not in seen` where seen is a list. That is about 200,000²/2 = 20 billion comparisons. At roughly 50 million per second in CPython, that takes around 400 s. Switching to a set makes it 200,000 hash lookups, well under a second. Replacing `sorted(scores)[-20:]` with heapq.nlargest(20, scores) avoids sorting everything on each query.
mistakes: Membership checks on lists inside loops.
Sorting everything to take the top few items.
Recursion without memoization on overlapping subproblems.
Running backtracking regexes on untrusted, unbounded input.
lesson.enterprise: A ticket-routing service slows to 40 s per batch as volume grows. A profile shows a nested loop matching every ticket against every rule. Indexing rules by keyword in a dict and capping input length brings the batch to under 1 s, and switching the rule engine to RE2 removes a backtracking risk found in review.
takeaways: Choose the structure that makes the dominant operation cheap.
Know the big-O of dict, set, list, deque and heap operations.
Graphs and topological sort model plans, pipelines and lineage.
Algorithmic complexity is a security property when attackers choose the input.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart TD
  Q{"Dominant operation?"} -->|"seen it?"| H["dict / set: O(1)"]
  Q -->|"best k?"| HP["heap: O(n log k)"]
  Q -->|"FIFO work"| D["deque: O(1) ends"]
  Q -->|"range / position"| B["sorted list + bisect: O(log n)"]
  Q -->|"what first?"| G["graph + topological sort"]
lesson.diagramAlt: A decision tree that maps the dominant operation to a data structure: membership to dict or set, best-k to a heap, FIFO work to a deque, range queries to a sorted list with bisect, and ordering dependencies to a graph with topological sort.

case.title: Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019
case.summary: Cloudflare deployed a new WAF managed rule containing a regular expression that backtracked enormously. It exhausted CPU on every core handling HTTP/HTTPS traffic across its network, bringing down core proxying, CDN and WAF functionality for 27 minutes. The post-mortem explains regex backtracking in detail and the process gaps that slowed the response.
case.lesson: Algorithmic complexity is an availability risk. Use linear-time matching for untrusted input, and stage global rule rollouts.

subjects.title: Git, Linux and the Command Line
subjects.why: FDEs and AI engineers debug on customer boxes, GPU nodes and CI runners. The shell and Git are the universal tools there.
subjects.explainer:
You will SSH into a VM inside a customer's VPC, read logs on a GPU node, bisect a regression and rescue a broken branch, often with no GUI. Fluency means: navigating and inspecting a Linux system (processes, ports, disk, permissions, systemd, environment variables), composing pipelines with grep, awk, jq and xargs, writing safe bash scripts, and using Git beyond add/commit/push (branches, rebase vs merge, bisect, reflog, tags, signed commits).

Safety habits matter as much as speed: know which host you're on, prefer dry runs, and never run destructive commands you haven't read twice.

resources.title: Pro Git (official book)
resources.why: The free, community-updated Pro Git book. Chapters 2–3 (basics, branching) and 7 (tools, including reset, rerere and bisect) cover what you need daily.

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education (MIT)
resources.why: MIT's course on the tools nobody teaches: shell, scripting, editors, data wrangling, command-line environment, version control and debugging.

resources.title: Learn Git Branching
resources.why: An interactive visual sandbox where you run Git commands and watch the commit graph change. The fastest way to understand rebase and cherry-pick.

resources.title: GNU Bash Reference Manual
resources.why: The official Bash 5.3 manual: expansions, quoting, redirections, conditionals and the set builtin options used in safe scripts.

resources.title: GitLab: Postmortem of database outage of January 31 (2017)
resources.why: A candid post-mortem: a deletion meant for the secondary ran on the primary, about 300 GB was removed, and several backup methods turned out not to work.

subjects.project: Write a safe bash script (set -euo pipefail, dry-run flag, host check) that collects diagnostics from a Linux VM, and use git bisect to find the commit that broke a test in a sample repo.

topics.title: Linux and shell fluency
topics.explainer: Linux skills for AI work are diagnostic. Which process holds the port (ss -ltnp)? Why is the disk full (df -h, du -sh)? Is the service running (systemctl status, journalctl -u)? Which environment variables did the container get? Pipelines turn logs into answers: grep for errors, jq to slice JSON logs, sort | uniq -c for counts. For scripts, start with set -euo pipefail, quote variables, and add a --dry-run mode. Permissions, users and file ownership explain a large share of 'works locally, fails on the server' bugs.

subtopics.title: Process, port and disk triage
subtopics.text: ps, top, ss -ltnp, df -h, du -sh and free -h answer most 'why is it slow or broken' questions.

subtopics.title: systemd and logs
subtopics.text: systemctl status and journalctl -u <service> show whether a service is up and why it died.

subtopics.title: Pipelines with grep, jq and awk
subtopics.text: Compose small tools: jq for JSON logs, sort | uniq -c for counts, xargs for batch actions.

subtopics.title: Safe bash scripting
subtopics.text: Use set -euo pipefail, quote variables, check the hostname and support --dry-run before destructive steps.

topics.title: Git beyond the basics
topics.explainer: Git is your undo button and your audit log. Learn the model first: commits are snapshots, branches are movable pointers, and HEAD is where you are. Then the rescue tools: git reflog recovers 'lost' commits, git bisect binary-searches history for the commit that broke something, and git revert undoes a pushed change safely, unlike rewriting shared history. Agree on a team workflow (trunk-based with short-lived branches is common), protect main with required reviews and CI, and never commit secrets: once pushed, assume they are leaked and rotate them.

subtopics.title: The commit graph
subtopics.text: Commits are snapshots, branches are pointers; draw the graph when a merge or rebase confuses you.

subtopics.title: bisect and reflog
subtopics.text: git bisect finds a bad commit in log2(n) steps; git reflog recovers commits after a bad reset.

subtopics.title: Merge, rebase and revert
subtopics.text: Rebase only private branches; use revert to undo commits that others already have.

subtopics.title: Secrets and hygiene
subtopics.text: Use .gitignore, pre-commit secret scanning and rotation; deleting a pushed secret does not un-leak it.

quiz.q: A test started failing somewhere in the last 200 commits. Fastest systematic approach?
choices: Revert the last commit and hope
quiz.why: Binary search over 200 commits needs about log2(200) ≈ 8 steps.

quiz.q: What does `set -euo pipefail` do in a bash script?
choices: Exit on errors, unset variables and failures inside pipelines
quiz.why: It turns silent failures into immediate exits.

quiz.q: You accidentally pushed an API key. What must you do?
choices: Rotate the key, then remove it from history
Delete the file in a new commit and move on
Make the repo private and keep the key
quiz.why: Assume anything pushed is compromised; rotation is the real fix.

lesson.intuition: The command line is a workshop where small, sharp tools snap together. Git is a time machine with a full logbook. Together they let you inspect any system, automate any chore and undo almost any mistake, provided you know which machine you're standing on and you keep the logbook honest.
how: Orient: whoami, hostname, pwd and environment before acting.
Inspect: processes, ports, disk, services and logs.
Compose: pipe small tools together to answer one question at a time.
Script safely: strict mode, quoting, dry-run and host checks.
Version everything: small commits, protected main, bisect and revert for recovery.
lesson.example: A model server on a customer VM returns 502s. Running ss -ltnp shows nothing listening on :8000. journalctl -u model-server shows 'CUDA out of memory' at startup. Running nvidia-smi shows a stale process holding 70 GB, which you stop. Back in the repo, git bisect over the last 64 commits takes 6 runs and finds a commit that doubled max_model_len. You revert it with git revert and push.
lesson.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Collect diagnostics safely from a Linux host. Usage: ./diag.sh [--dry-run] expected-hostname
set -euo pipefail
DRY=0; [[ "${1:-}" == "--dry-run" ]] && { DRY=1; shift; }
EXPECTED="${1:?usage: diag.sh [--dry-run] expected-hostname}"
[[ "$(hostname)" == "$EXPECTED" ]] || { echo "refusing: on $(hostname), expected $EXPECTED" >&2; exit 1; }
run() { if (( DRY )); then echo "[dry-run] $*"; else "$@"; fi; }
OUT="diag-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"; run mkdir -p "$OUT"
run sh -c "df -h > '$OUT/disk.txt'"
run sh -c "ss -ltnp > '$OUT/ports.txt' 2>/dev/null || true"
run sh -c "journalctl -u model-server --since '1 hour ago' --no-pager > '$OUT/service.log' 2>/dev/null || true"
run sh -c "grep -c -i error '$OUT/service.log' || true"
echo "done: $OUT"
# Find the commit that broke the tests in about log2(N) steps:
#   git bisect start HEAD v1.4.0 && git bisect run pytest -q tests/test_api.py && git bisect reset
mistakes: Running destructive commands without checking which host you are on.
Scripts without strict mode that keep going after a failure.
Rewriting shared history with force-push instead of reverting.
Committing .env files and API keys.
lesson.enterprise: An FDE team standardizes a diagnostics script and a 'host banner' prompt that shows the environment name in red for production. Combined with protected branches and required CI, incidents caused by commands run on the wrong host drop to zero over two quarters.
takeaways: Orient before you act: hostname, user and environment.
Strict-mode bash with dry-run is the minimum for automation.
bisect, reflog and revert are your recovery tools.
Treat any pushed secret as leaked and rotate it.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  O["Orient: hostname, whoami"] --> I["Inspect: ps, ss, df, journalctl"]
  I --> P["Pipe: grep | jq | sort | uniq -c"]
  P --> F["Fix with a safe script (dry-run first)"]
  F --> G["Commit + PR + CI"]
  G -->|"regression?"| B["git bisect"]
  B --> RV["git revert"]
lesson.diagramAlt: Flow from orienting on a host, inspecting processes, ports, disk and logs, piping tools to find the cause, fixing it with a dry-run-first script, then committing through a pull request with CI, and using git bisect and git revert when a regression appears.

case.title: Postmortem of database outage of January 31 (GitLab, 2017)
case.summary: While fighting replication problems, a GitLab engineer ran a data-removal process meant for the secondary database on the primary (db1). By the time they stopped it a second or two later, about 300 GB of data had been removed. Finding and using backups then failed. The restore relied on a manual snapshot taken about 6 hours earlier, which was copied to staging.
case.lesson: Make it obvious which host you're on, and test restores, not just backups. A safe environment is one where mistakes are quick to recover from.

subjects.title: Debugging Systematically
subjects.why: AI systems fail in layered ways (network, auth, data, prompt, model). A disciplined debugging loop finds the layer quickly instead of guessing.
subjects.explainer:
Debugging is the scientific method applied to software. Reproduce the failure. Shrink it to the smallest case. Form a hypothesis. Change one thing. Observe. With LLM systems, there are more layers to check: is it the network, the auth token, the retrieved context, the prompt template, the model version, the parser, or the tool?

Tools help (debuggers such as pdb and DevTools, structured logs, traces, the USE method for resources), but the habit matters more: read the actual error, check assumptions, and write down what you have ruled out.

resources.title: Julia Evans: A debugging manifesto
resources.why: A short list of debugging attitudes from Julia Evans' zine: inspect, don't guess; trust nothing; the bug is happening for a logical reason; it's probably your code.

resources.title: pdb: The Python Debugger (Python docs)
resources.why: Breakpoints (including conditional ones), stepping, stack inspection and post-mortem debugging. breakpoint() enters pdb from any line.

resources.title: Brendan Gregg: The USE Method
resources.why: A checklist approach to performance: for every resource, check utilization, saturation and errors. Includes per-OS metric lists you can apply to GPU nodes.

resources.title: Chrome DevTools: Debug JavaScript
resources.why: A step-by-step tutorial on breakpoints, stepping and watch expressions in DevTools, for debugging TypeScript and JavaScript front ends.

subjects.project: Take a failing agent trace, reproduce it deterministically by pinning the model, seed and inputs, bisect the layers (retrieval, prompt, model, parser), and write a one-page incident note with the root cause and a regression test.

topics.title: The debugging loop
topics.explainer: A reliable loop: reproduce, minimize, hypothesize, test, fix, and prevent. Reproducing an LLM bug means capturing the exact inputs: prompt, retrieved chunks, tool outputs, model name and version, temperature and seed. Minimizing means deleting context until the bug disappears, which shows you the trigger. Hypotheses should be falsifiable ('the date parser fails on ISO week formats'). Change one variable at a time. After the fix, add a regression test or eval case so the bug can't silently return. Keep notes; they become the post-mortem.

subtopics.title: Reproduce deterministically
subtopics.text: Capture inputs, versions and settings; set temperature to 0 or pin a seed when the API allows it.

subtopics.title: Minimize the case
subtopics.text: Remove context, tools and steps until the failure disappears; the last removal is the clue.

subtopics.title: One change at a time
subtopics.text: Change a single variable per experiment so each result is interpretable.

subtopics.title: Prevent recurrence
subtopics.text: Turn every fixed bug into a unit test or eval case.

topics.title: Tools and layered diagnosis
topics.explainer: Pick the tool for the layer. For code, use an interactive debugger (pdb or breakpoint() in Python, Chrome DevTools for TypeScript) to inspect state at the failing line. For services, use structured logs and distributed traces to see which hop failed and how long each took. For resources, use Brendan Gregg's USE method: for every resource, check utilization, saturation and errors. For LLM behaviour, diff the prompt that worked against the one that failed, and replay traces against a pinned model. Work outside-in: network and auth first, then data, then prompt and model.

subtopics.title: Interactive debuggers
subtopics.text: breakpoint() drops into pdb; DevTools breakpoints and watch expressions do the same in the browser.

subtopics.title: Logs and traces
subtopics.text: Structured logs with request IDs and spans show where time and errors occur.

subtopics.title: USE method
subtopics.text: Utilization, saturation and errors for CPU, memory, disk, network and GPU locate resource bottlenecks.

subtopics.title: Prompt and trace diffs
subtopics.text: Compare a good and a bad trace side by side; the difference is usually in retrieved context or the template.

quiz.q: An agent gives a wrong answer 1 time in 20. First step?
choices: Capture full traces of failures and reproduce one deterministically
Rewrite the system prompt from scratch
quiz.why: You can't fix what you can't reproduce; traces give you the exact inputs.

quiz.q: What does the USE method check for each resource?
quiz.why: Brendan Gregg's USE method is a checklist for resource bottlenecks.

quiz.q: After fixing a parsing bug, what prevents it from returning?
choices: A regression test or eval case built from the failing input
quiz.why: Bugs that aren't tested come back.

lesson.intuition: Debugging is detective work with a strict rule: no accusations without evidence. A bug feels mysterious only because one of your assumptions is wrong. Reproduce the crime, narrow down the suspects (network, auth, data, prompt, model, parser), and test one alibi at a time until a single explanation is left.
how: Reproduce: capture exact inputs, versions and settings.
Minimize: strip the case down until the bug disappears.
Locate the layer: network → auth → data → prompt → model → parser → tool.
Hypothesize and test one change at a time.
Fix, add a regression test or eval, and write a short note.
lesson.example: A contract-QA agent cites the wrong clause about 5% of the time. Traces show every failure involves PDFs with two-column layouts. Minimizing to one page reproduces it: the parser interleaves the columns, so chunks mix clauses. The model and prompt were fine. Switching the parser to a layout-aware mode and adding 10 two-column pages to the eval set fixes it, and the eval now guards against regressions.
lesson.code:
# Minimize a failing input automatically (a tiny delta-debugging loop), then keep it as a regression test.
def buggy_parse(lines):
    # Bug: a line starting with "|" (a table row) is treated as a heading.
    return [l for l in lines if not l.startswith("|")]
def fails(lines):
    return len(buggy_parse(lines)) != len(lines)     # oracle: no line should be dropped
def minimize(case):
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for i in range(len(case)):
            smaller = case[:i] + case[i+1:]
            if smaller and fails(smaller):
                case, changed = smaller, True
                break
    return case
doc = ["# Terms", "Payment within 30 days.", "| fee | 2% |", "Termination with notice.", "## Annex"]
assert fails(doc)
minimal = minimize(doc)
print("minimal failing input:", minimal)
assert minimal == ["| fee | 2% |"]
# This minimal case becomes the regression test: assert not fails(["| fee | 2% |"]) after the fix.
mistakes: Changing several things at once, then not knowing which one helped.
Blaming the model before checking retrieval, auth and parsing.
Debugging without traces or captured inputs.
Fixing the bug without adding a test, so it comes back.
lesson.enterprise: A bank's document assistant sees accuracy drop after a vendor update. The team replays 200 stored traces against the old and new model versions with identical retrieval and finds the drop is entirely in table-heavy questions. They pin the previous model for that route while they tune the prompt, and add 40 table questions to the eval gate.
takeaways: Reproduce before you fix; capture full inputs and versions.
Work outside-in through the layers.
Change one variable per experiment.
Every fixed bug becomes a test or eval case.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  R["Reproduce"] --> M["Minimize"]
  M --> L{"Which layer?"}
  L --> N["Network / auth"]
  L --> D["Data / retrieval"]
  L --> P["Prompt / model"]
  L --> X["Parser / tool"]
  N --> H["Hypothesis → one change"]
  D --> H
  P --> H
  X --> H
  H --> F["Fix + regression test"]
lesson.diagramAlt: The debugging loop: reproduce, minimize, then decide which layer fails (network and auth, data and retrieval, prompt and model, or parser and tool), form a hypothesis tested with one change, and finish with a fix plus a regression test.

subjects.title: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC
subjects.why: Agents and integrations consume APIs all day. Picking and using the right API style affects latency, token cost and how much glue code you write.
subjects.explainer:
Three styles dominate. REST models resources with HTTP methods and status codes: it's universal, cacheable and the default for public and partner APIs. GraphQL exposes a typed schema where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one round trip, which suits UIs and agents that need shaped data from many related objects. gRPC uses Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 for fast, strongly typed, streaming service-to-service calls.

For AI work, the choice shows up as round trips, payload size (tokens!), schema discoverability for tool generation, and streaming support.

resources.title: GraphQL: Learn
resources.why: The official GraphQL lessons: queries, mutations, schemas and types, validation, execution and best practices, including how GraphQL enables versionless APIs.

resources.title: Introduction to gRPC
resources.why: gRPC's overview of Protocol Buffers as the IDL and message format, service definitions and generated clients across languages.

resources.title: MDN: HTTP request methods
resources.why: Each HTTP method's semantics, plus the safe, idempotent and cacheable properties that REST APIs and retry logic rely on.

resources.title: Fielding's dissertation, Chapter 5: REST
resources.why: The original definition of the REST architectural style and its constraints (client-server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, layered system).

resources.title: GitHub: The GitHub GraphQL API (2016)
resources.why: Why GitHub added GraphQL: the REST API drove over 60% of database-tier requests, partly because hypermedia navigation forces repeated round trips.

subjects.project: Expose the same 'customer with last 5 orders' data as a REST endpoint, a GraphQL query and a gRPC method, then compare round trips, payload bytes and the tokens each response would cost an agent.

topics.title: Three styles and when to use each
topics.explainer: REST is resource-oriented: GET /customers/42, POST /orders, with HTTP semantics (safe and idempotent methods, status codes, caching headers). It's the lingua franca of SaaS integrations. GraphQL puts one endpoint in front of a typed graph; clients write queries naming the fields they want, which avoids over-fetching and chains of requests, but it moves complexity to the server (query cost limits, N+1 resolution, caching). gRPC defines services in .proto files and generates clients; it's efficient and supports bidirectional streaming, which is why it's common inside platforms and inference servers.

subtopics.title: REST and HTTP semantics
subtopics.text: GET is safe, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is neither; status codes and caching headers carry meaning.

subtopics.title: GraphQL queries and schema
subtopics.text: Clients select fields from a typed schema in one request; introspection documents the API.

subtopics.title: gRPC and Protocol Buffers
subtopics.text: Contract-first .proto definitions, generated clients, HTTP/2 and streaming for internal services.

subtopics.title: Choosing
subtopics.text: Public or partner APIs: REST. Rich UI or agent data needs: GraphQL. Internal high-throughput or streaming: gRPC.

topics.title: APIs as agent tools
topics.explainer: When an agent calls an API, every byte of the response becomes tokens. A REST endpoint returning a 40 KB customer object for a question that needs two fields wastes context and money. GraphQL's field selection, or a thin wrapper tool that projects only the needed fields, fixes that. Schemas matter too: OpenAPI documents and GraphQL introspection can be turned into tool definitions automatically, but the result is usually too broad. Curate a few task-shaped tools, add pagination and filters, and return compact, well-labelled results with clear errors.

subtopics.title: Token cost of payloads
subtopics.text: Project responses to the fields the task needs; large JSON blobs crowd out reasoning context.

subtopics.title: Schema-to-tool generation
subtopics.text: OpenAPI and GraphQL schemas can generate tools, but curate them into a small, task-shaped set.

subtopics.title: Pagination and filtering
subtopics.text: Give tools limit, cursor and filter parameters so agents don't pull entire collections.

subtopics.title: Errors agents can act on
subtopics.text: Return structured errors (for example RFC 9457 problem details) that say what to fix.

quiz.q: A UI needs a customer, their last 5 orders and each order's items. REST needs 7 calls. Which style reduces round trips by design?
quiz.why: GraphQL lets one query select nested related data.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method is idempotent by definition?
quiz.why: PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.

quiz.q: Why does response size matter more when an agent is the client?
choices: Every byte becomes tokens that cost money and context
quiz.why: Tool outputs are fed back into the context window.

lesson.intuition: REST is a library with a shelf per resource: you fetch whole books one at a time. GraphQL is a librarian you hand a precise list to, and you get exactly those pages in one trip. gRPC is a pneumatic tube between two departments that agreed on the form in advance: fast and typed, but internal.
how: List the consumers: public partners, UIs, agents or internal services.
Match the style: REST for broad compatibility, GraphQL for shaped data, gRPC for internal speed and streaming.
Define the contract first (OpenAPI, GraphQL schema or .proto).
For agent tools, project responses to the needed fields and add pagination.
Return structured errors and document limits.
lesson.example: An agent answers 'when did customer 42's last 5 orders ship?'. With REST it calls GET /customers/42 (8 KB), then 5 × GET /orders/{id} (6 KB each): 6 calls, 38 KB, about 9,500 tokens. A GraphQL query for customer(id:42){orders(last:5){id shippedAt}} is 1 call and about 300 bytes, roughly 75 tokens. At $3 per million input tokens and 100,000 questions a month, that's about $2,850 vs $23.
lesson.code:
import json
# Compare the payload an agent must read for one question: REST chain vs a GraphQL-style field selection.
customer = {"id": 42, "name": "Acme", "address": {"street": "1 Main", "city": "Detroit"}, "notes": "x" * 2000,
            "orders": [{"id": f"O-{i}", "shippedAt": f"2026-10-0{i}", "items": [{"sku": "S1", "desc": "y" * 900}] * 5} for i in range(1, 6)]}
rest_calls = [json.dumps({k: v for k, v in customer.items() if k != "orders"})] + [json.dumps(o) for o in customer["orders"]]
def select(obj, fields):
    """Tiny GraphQL-like projection: fields is a dict of name -> sub-selection (or None)."""
    if isinstance(obj, list): return [select(o, fields) for o in obj]
    return {k: (select(obj[k], sub) if sub else obj[k]) for k, sub in fields.items()}
gql = json.dumps(select(customer, {"id": None, "orders": {"id": None, "shippedAt": None}}))
rest_bytes = sum(len(c) for c in rest_calls)
tok = lambda b: b // 4                     # rough: ~4 bytes per token
print(f"REST: {len(rest_calls)} calls, {rest_bytes} bytes, ~{tok(rest_bytes)} tokens")
print(f"GraphQL-style: 1 call, {len(gql)} bytes, ~{tok(len(gql))} tokens")
print(gql)
mistakes: Exposing a raw REST API as an agent tool and letting it pull huge objects.
Adopting GraphQL without query cost limits or depth limits.
Using gRPC for public browser-facing APIs without a gateway.
Ignoring HTTP semantics (using POST for everything), which breaks retries and caching.
lesson.enterprise: A CRM vendor's agent integration pulls full account objects through REST and hits context limits on large accounts. Wrapping the API in three task-shaped tools backed by GraphQL field selection cuts tool-output tokens by about 85% and removes the context-overflow errors.
takeaways: REST for broad compatibility, GraphQL for shaped data, gRPC for internal speed.
Respect HTTP semantics; retries and caches depend on them.
For agents, response size is cost and context.
Contract-first schemas enable generated clients and tools.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C["Client"] -->|"GET /customers/42"| R1["REST"]
  C -->|"GET /orders/1..5 (5 calls)"| R1
  C -->|"one query, chosen fields"| G["GraphQL"]
  S1["Service A"] <-->|"protobuf over HTTP/2, streaming"| GR["gRPC"]
  GR <--> S2["Service B"]
lesson.diagramAlt: A client makes six REST calls to get a customer and five orders, or a single GraphQL query that selects only the needed fields. Two internal services exchange Protocol Buffer messages over HTTP/2 with gRPC streaming.

case.title: The GitHub GraphQL API (GitHub Blog, 2016)
case.summary: GitHub announced a GraphQL API alongside its widely copied REST API. One motivation was scalability: the REST API was responsible for over 60% of the requests made to its database tier, partly because hypermedia navigation requires clients to make repeated requests to collect what they need. GitHub implemented the schema with the graphql-ruby gem and used Shopify's graphql-batch to fetch related records efficiently.
case.lesson: When clients need connected data, letting them ask for exactly what they need in one request can cut round trips and backend load. You then have to handle batching and query cost.

subjects.title: PostgreSQL for AI Engineers: Indexing, Transactions and pgvector
subjects.why: Postgres is the default system of record behind most AI products, and with pgvector it is often the vector store too. Indexes and transactions decide correctness and latency.
subjects.explainer:
Postgres stores users, conversations, tool results, audit logs, feature flags and, with the pgvector extension, embeddings. Three skills matter. Modeling: normalized tables with constraints, plus JSONB where flexibility genuinely helps. Indexing: B-tree for equality and range, GIN for JSONB and full-text, and HNSW or IVFFlat for vectors, always verified with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Transactions: atomic multi-step writes, isolation levels, row locks and idempotent upserts with ON CONFLICT.

Most 'the database is slow' problems are a missing index, an N+1 query pattern or a long-running transaction holding locks.

resources.title: PostgreSQL docs: Chapter 11, Indexes
resources.why: Official chapter on index types (B-tree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN, BRIN), multicolumn, partial and expression indexes, and index-only scans.

resources.title: PostgreSQL docs: 13.2 Transaction Isolation
resources.why: Exactly which anomalies each isolation level allows in Postgres, and why SERIALIZABLE transactions can fail and must be retried.

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke
resources.why: Markus Winand's free developer-focused guide to SQL indexing: how B-trees work, composite index column order, and why some queries can't use an index.

resources.title: pgvector
resources.why: Vector types, distance operators, HNSW and IVFFlat indexes, and how filtering interacts with approximate search in Postgres.

resources.title: Notion: Herding elephants, lessons learned from sharding Postgres (2021)
resources.why: How Notion split its Postgres monolith into 480 logical shards on 32 physical databases, with double-writes, an audit log and a short maintenance window.

subjects.project: Design a schema for conversations, messages and document chunks with embeddings in Postgres. Add B-tree, GIN and HNSW indexes, prove each one with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and implement an idempotent ingestion upsert inside a transaction.

topics.title: Modeling and indexing
topics.explainer: Model the core entities relationally, with primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL and CHECK constraints, so the database itself rejects bad data. Use JSONB for genuinely variable attributes such as tool outputs, not as a way to skip modeling. Indexes trade write cost and disk for read speed. A B-tree on (tenant_id, created_at) serves 'latest messages for a tenant'. A GIN index serves JSONB containment and full-text search. pgvector adds HNSW and IVFFlat indexes for approximate nearest-neighbour search. Always confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the planner actually uses the index you added.

subtopics.title: Constraints as guardrails
subtopics.text: Foreign keys, NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK constraints stop bad data at the source.

subtopics.title: B-tree and composite indexes
subtopics.text: Order composite index columns by how queries filter: equality columns first, then range or sort columns.

subtopics.title: GIN, JSONB and full-text
subtopics.text: GIN indexes accelerate JSONB containment (@>) and tsvector full-text search.

subtopics.title: pgvector HNSW and filters
subtopics.text: HNSW gives fast approximate search; combine it with WHERE filters such as tenant_id and check recall.

topics.title: Transactions, isolation and locks
topics.explainer: A transaction makes several writes succeed or fail together: insert the message, update the conversation's last_message_at and record the token usage, or none of them. Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED isolation. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE give stronger guarantees but may abort transactions, which your code must retry. Use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE for idempotent upserts, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED to build safe job queues, and keep transactions short: an idle transaction holds locks and blocks vacuum. Connection pooling (PgBouncer) protects the database from many short-lived app connections.

subtopics.title: Atomicity
subtopics.text: Group related writes in one transaction so a crash can't leave half-updated state.

subtopics.title: Isolation levels
subtopics.text: READ COMMITTED by default; SERIALIZABLE prevents anomalies but requires retrying serialization failures.

subtopics.title: Upserts and SKIP LOCKED
subtopics.text: ON CONFLICT makes ingestion idempotent; FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets many workers claim jobs safely.

subtopics.title: Pooling and long transactions
subtopics.text: Pool connections and keep transactions short to avoid lock pile-ups and bloat.

quiz.q: A query filters `WHERE tenant_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`. Best index?
quiz.why: Equality column first, then the sort column, lets Postgres read just 20 rows.

quiz.q: How do you make re-ingesting the same document safe to run twice?
choices: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (doc_id, chunk_no) DO UPDATE
DELETE all rows first without a transaction
Rely on the application to remember
quiz.why: An upsert on a natural key makes the operation idempotent.

quiz.q: You added an index but the query is still slow. What do you check?
choices: EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see whether the planner uses it
quiz.why: The plan shows whether the index is used and where time goes.

lesson.intuition: Postgres is a careful accountant. Constraints are the rules it refuses to break, indexes are the tabs in its ledger that let it find a page without reading the whole book, and transactions are its promise that a set of entries is either fully written or never happened.
how: Model entities with keys and constraints; use JSONB only for genuinely variable data.
Write the important queries first, then design indexes for them.
Verify every index with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on realistic data.
Wrap multi-step writes in short transactions; use upserts for idempotency.
Pool connections and monitor slow queries, locks and bloat.
lesson.example: A chat app's 'load conversation' query takes 1.8 s for big tenants: Postgres scans 3M messages and sorts them. Adding CREATE INDEX ON messages (tenant_id, conversation_id, created_at DESC) changes the plan to an index scan returning 50 rows in 4 ms. For RAG, an HNSW index on embedding with WHERE tenant_id = $1 returns the top 10 in about 15 ms instead of a 900 ms exact scan.
lesson.code:
import sqlite3, time
# Same ideas in SQLite (stdlib) so it runs anywhere: composite index, query plan, idempotent upsert in a transaction.
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE messages(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id INT NOT NULL, conv_id INT NOT NULL,
                      created_at INT NOT NULL, body TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE chunks(doc_id TEXT, chunk_no INT, text TEXT, PRIMARY KEY(doc_id, chunk_no));
""")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO messages(tenant_id, conv_id, created_at, body) VALUES (?,?,?,?)",
               ((t % 50, t % 900, t, "hi") for t in range(200_000)))
q = "SELECT body FROM messages WHERE tenant_id=7 AND conv_id=7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20"
def timed():
    t = time.perf_counter(); db.execute(q).fetchall(); return (time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000
before = timed()
db.execute("CREATE INDEX ix_msg ON messages(tenant_id, conv_id, created_at DESC)")
after = timed()
print("plan:", db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + q).fetchall()[0][-1])
print(f"before {before:.1f} ms, after {after:.2f} ms")
def ingest(doc_id, chunks):
    with db:                                   # one transaction: all chunks or none
        db.executemany("INSERT INTO chunks VALUES (?,?,?) ON CONFLICT(doc_id, chunk_no) DO UPDATE SET text=excluded.text",
                       [(doc_id, i, c) for i, c in enumerate(chunks)])
ingest("policy", ["a", "b"]); ingest("policy", ["a", "b2"])   # re-run is safe
print(db.execute("SELECT * FROM chunks").fetchall())
# Postgres + pgvector equivalent:  CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
mistakes: Adding indexes without checking EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
Storing everything in one JSONB column to avoid modeling.
Long-running or idle-in-transaction sessions holding locks.
Vector search without tenant filters, which leaks data across customers.
lesson.enterprise: A SaaS team keeps embeddings in Postgres with pgvector rather than adding a separate vector database. With an HNSW index, a tenant_id filter and nightly recall checks against exact search, they keep p95 retrieval under 30 ms for 40M chunks, and get transactions, backups and row-level security from the database they already run.
takeaways: Constraints make the database a guardrail, not just storage.
Design indexes for real queries and prove them with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
Short transactions plus upserts give correctness and idempotency.
pgvector is often enough; filter by tenant and measure recall.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  APP["App / agent"] --> POOL["PgBouncer pool"]
  POOL --> PG[("PostgreSQL")]
  PG --> BT["B-tree: tenant_id, created_at"]
  PG --> GIN["GIN: JSONB / full-text"]
  PG --> HNSW["HNSW: pgvector embeddings"]
  APP -->|"BEGIN ... upsert ... COMMIT"| POOL
lesson.diagramAlt: An app connects through a PgBouncer pool to PostgreSQL, which uses a B-tree index for tenant and time filters, a GIN index for JSONB and full-text search, and an HNSW index for pgvector embeddings. Writes are grouped into transactions with upserts.

case.title: Herding elephants: Lessons learned from sharding Postgres at Notion (2021)
case.summary: Notion sharded its monolithic Postgres database into 480 logical shards, each a Postgres schema, spread evenly across 32 physical databases (15 per database), partitioned so related data stays together. The migration used double-writes with an audit log and a catch-up script. The final cutover took Notion down for five minutes of scheduled maintenance.
case.lesson: Choose partition keys that keep related data and transactions on one host, and plan migrations around double-writes and verification.

subjects.title: MongoDB and Document Stores
subjects.why: Many customer systems, and many agent memory and logging stores, are document databases. Knowing when documents beat tables, and how to model them, avoids painful migrations.
subjects.explainer:
Document databases such as MongoDB store JSON-like documents with flexible schemas, rich nested structures and horizontal scaling. They shine when an entity is naturally read and written as a whole (a product with variants, a conversation with its messages, an agent run with its steps), and when the shape varies between records.

The central skill is modeling for access patterns: embed what you read together, reference what grows without bound or is shared. Know the trade-offs too: single-document writes are atomic, multi-document transactions exist but cost more, and schema validation is opt-in. MongoDB Atlas also offers vector search, so documents and embeddings can live together.

resources.title: MongoDB: Data Modeling
resources.why: MongoDB's data modeling guide: flexible schema design, embedding vs referencing, and designing schemas around application use cases.

resources.title: MongoDB: Transactions
resources.why: Explains that single-document operations are atomic, when multi-document transactions are needed, and their production considerations.

resources.title: MongoDB Vector Search overview
resources.why: How to create vector indexes in MongoDB and run semantic and hybrid search, keeping embeddings next to operational documents.

resources.title: Discord: How Discord stores billions of messages
resources.why: Discord's account of starting on a single MongoDB replica set, hitting RAM and latency limits at 100 million messages, and moving to Cassandra with time buckets.

subjects.project: Model agent runs (steps, tool calls, costs) in a document store: embed bounded step arrays, reference large artifacts, add JSON Schema validation and a compound index, then compare with the equivalent Postgres JSONB design.

topics.title: Modeling for access patterns
topics.explainer: Start from the queries, not the entities. If the app always loads a conversation with its last 50 messages, embedding recent messages in the conversation document gives one read. If a channel's messages grow forever, embedding them will eventually exceed document size limits (16 MB in MongoDB) and slow every update, so reference them in a separate collection, bucketed by time. Duplicate small, rarely changing fields (such as a user's display name) to avoid joins, and accept that updates then touch several documents. Turn on schema validation for fields your code depends on.

subtopics.title: Embed vs reference
subtopics.text: Embed data read together and bounded in size; reference data that is shared or grows without bound.

subtopics.title: Bucketing unbounded data
subtopics.text: Group time-series or chat data into buckets (per day or per N items) to cap document size.

subtopics.title: Schema validation
subtopics.text: Use $jsonSchema validators so required fields and types are enforced by the database.

subtopics.title: Compound indexes
subtopics.text: Index fields in the order queries filter and sort, as in relational databases.

topics.title: Consistency, transactions and choosing a store
topics.explainer: In MongoDB a single-document write is atomic, which is why good document models put data that must change together into one document. Multi-document ACID transactions exist but add latency and coordination, so frequent use is a signal the data might be relational. Read and write concerns control durability and consistency across a replica set. Choose a document store for variable, hierarchical, document-shaped data with clear access patterns. Choose Postgres when you need many-to-many relationships, ad-hoc joins and strong constraints. Postgres JSONB is a middle ground for occasional flexibility.

subtopics.title: Single-document atomicity
subtopics.text: Design documents so one logical change is one document write.

subtopics.title: Multi-document transactions
subtopics.text: Available, but costlier; frequent need suggests a relational model.

subtopics.title: Read and write concerns
subtopics.text: writeConcern majority and readConcern majority trade latency for durability and consistency.

subtopics.title: Document store vs Postgres
subtopics.text: Variable, nested, access-pattern-driven data favours documents; relationships and constraints favour Postgres.

quiz.q: A chat channel's messages grow forever. How should they be stored in a document database?
choices: Separate collection, bucketed by channel and time
One array inside the channel document
quiz.why: Unbounded arrays hit size limits and slow updates; bucket them.

quiz.q: Which write is atomic in MongoDB without an explicit transaction?
choices: Any write to a single document, including nested fields
quiz.why: Single-document operations are atomic, so model data that changes together into one document.

quiz.q: Strong signal you should use a relational database instead?
choices: Many ad-hoc joins and many-to-many relationships with strict constraints
Each record has a different shape
You read whole documents at once
quiz.why: Relational strengths are joins, relationships and constraints.

lesson.intuition: A document store is a filing cabinet of folders. Each folder holds everything about one thing, so you grab it in one motion. That is great when you always want the whole folder, and awkward when you constantly need to cross-reference pages between folders. A relational database is the opposite: neat index cards joined on demand.
how: List the read and write access patterns and their frequencies.
Embed data that is read together and bounded; reference data that is shared or unbounded.
Add schema validation for fields code depends on.
Create compound indexes for the main queries.
Keep logical changes inside one document; use transactions sparingly.
lesson.example: Agent runs average 12 steps, at most 200, at about 1 KB per step, so a run document stays under 200 KB. Embedding the steps lets the trace viewer load a run in one read. Large tool outputs (PDF extracts of up to 5 MB) go to object storage, with a reference in the step. An index on {tenant_id: 1, started_at: -1} serves the 'recent runs' list. The design avoids the 16 MB document limit with plenty of headroom.
mistakes: Embedding unbounded arrays such as all messages in a channel.
Using a document store but needing joins everywhere.
No schema validation, so every reader must handle every possible shape.
Assuming multi-document writes are atomic without a transaction.
lesson.enterprise: A retailer's product catalog has 40 categories with different attributes. Modeling products as documents with category-specific fields, plus validation for the shared core (sku, price, status), replaces a 200-column sparse table and lets an agent fetch a complete product in one read.
takeaways: Model for access patterns: embed together-read data, reference unbounded data.
Single-document writes are atomic; design around that.
Validate schemas in the database, even if they're flexible.
Choose documents for nested, variable data and Postgres for relationships.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart TD
  A{"Read together and bounded?"} -->|"yes"| E["Embed in parent document"]
  A -->|"no"| B{"Shared or unbounded?"}
  B -->|"unbounded"| BK["Separate collection, bucketed by time"]
  B -->|"shared"| RF["Reference by id"]
  E --> V["$jsonSchema validation + compound index"]
  BK --> V
  RF --> V
lesson.diagramAlt: A decision flow for document modeling: embed data that is read together and bounded; otherwise put unbounded data in a separate time-bucketed collection or reference shared data by id. All paths end with schema validation and compound indexes.

case.title: How Discord Stores Billions of Messages (Discord Engineering, 2017)
case.summary: Discord's first version, built in under two months in early 2015, stored everything in a single MongoDB replica set, deliberately planned for easy migration. Around November 2015 it reached 100 million stored messages. The data and index no longer fit in RAM and latencies became unpredictable. Discord moved messages to Cassandra, bucketing each channel's messages by time (about 10 days per bucket) to keep partitions under about 100 MB.
case.lesson: Start with what lets you iterate quickly, but plan the migration path. Model unbounded, growing data with buckets from the start.

subjects.title: Authentication and Authorization: OAuth2, OIDC, SAML SSO, RBAC and ABAC
subjects.why: Every enterprise deployment starts with 'it must use our SSO' and ends with 'the agent may only see what this user may see'. Identity is the first gate in every security review.
subjects.explainer:
Authentication answers who you are; authorization answers what you may do. In enterprises, authentication is delegated to an identity provider (Entra ID, Okta, Ping) via SAML 2.0 or OpenID Connect, so users sign in once. OAuth 2.0 issues scoped access tokens so an app or agent can call APIs on a user's behalf without seeing their password. Authorization models range from RBAC (roles grant permissions) to ABAC (policies over attributes of the user, resource and context) to relationship-based models (Zanzibar, OpenFGA).

For agents, the key rule is to act with the user's identity and the narrowest scopes, never with a shared superuser key.

resources.title: OAuth 2.0 (oauth.net)
resources.why: The community hub for OAuth 2.0: grant types, PKCE, token types and links to every relevant RFC and extension. Good orientation before reading specs.

resources.title: OpenID Foundation: How OpenID Connect Works
resources.why: Explains OIDC as an identity layer on OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749/6750): ID tokens, the UserInfo endpoint and how authentication by an authorization server is verified.

resources.title: OWASP SAML Security Cheat Sheet
resources.why: Concrete SAML hardening: validate signatures and the protocol, defend against XML signature wrapping, and IdP and SP considerations for SSO.

resources.title: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
resources.why: The IETF's current OAuth security guidance: PKCE everywhere, no implicit grant, sender-constrained and audience-restricted tokens, and refresh token protection.

resources.title: NIST: Attribute Based Access Control
resources.why: NIST's ABAC project page and guidance (SP 800-162), explaining ABAC's place among access control models and its policy and attribute components.

subjects.project: Add OIDC login (authorization code flow with PKCE) to a small web app, map IdP groups to roles, enforce an ABAC rule on documents, and show an agent tool call using a down-scoped, short-lived token.

topics.title: Authentication: SSO with SAML and OIDC
topics.explainer: Single sign-on lets employees use their corporate identity for your app. SAML 2.0 is XML-based and still dominant in enterprise SaaS: the identity provider (IdP) sends a signed assertion to your service provider (SP) after login. OpenID Connect is a JSON/JWT identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 and is preferred for new apps and mobile. Either way, verify signatures, audience, issuer and expiry; reject unsigned or replayed assertions; and support IdP-initiated and SP-initiated flows as customers require. SCIM provisioning keeps user accounts and group memberships in sync, including deprovisioning when someone leaves.

subtopics.title: SAML 2.0
subtopics.text: XML assertions signed by the IdP; validate signature, audience, recipient and NotOnOrAfter, and guard against XML signature wrapping.

subtopics.title: OpenID Connect
subtopics.text: ID tokens (JWT) from an OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE; verify iss, aud, exp and nonce.

subtopics.title: SCIM provisioning
subtopics.text: The IdP creates, updates and deactivates users and groups in your app automatically.

subtopics.title: MFA and session policy
subtopics.text: Leave MFA and conditional access to the IdP; keep app sessions short and revocable.

topics.title: Authorization: OAuth scopes, RBAC, ABAC and agents
topics.explainer: OAuth 2.0 lets a client obtain an access token with specific scopes, for example read:tickets, from an authorization server. Tokens should be short-lived, audience-restricted and refreshable. RBAC maps users to roles and roles to permissions: simple and auditable, but it explodes when access depends on context. ABAC evaluates policies over attributes, such as 'region = EU and clearance ≥ confidential and request during working hours', which suits data-dependent rules. For agents, use delegated tokens (on-behalf-of or token exchange per RFC 8693) so every tool call carries the user's permissions, and enforce authorization at the API or retrieval layer, never in the prompt.

subtopics.title: OAuth 2.0 scopes and tokens
subtopics.text: Short-lived, audience-bound access tokens with minimal scopes; refresh tokens stored securely.

subtopics.title: RBAC
subtopics.text: Users get roles, roles get permissions; map IdP groups to roles and review them regularly.

subtopics.title: ABAC
subtopics.text: Policies over user, resource and context attributes handle rules that roles can't express cleanly.

subtopics.title: Delegated access for agents
subtopics.text: Agents call tools with the user's down-scoped token; authorization is enforced by the system, not by the prompt.

quiz.q: An enterprise says 'use our Okta SSO'. Which protocols do you typically implement?
quiz.why: Enterprise SSO is almost always SAML or OIDC, often with SCIM for provisioning.

quiz.q: Where must 'the agent can only see documents this user can see' be enforced?
choices: In the retrieval and API layer, using the user's identity
By asking the model to be careful
quiz.why: Prompts are not security boundaries; enforce authorization in code and data access.

quiz.q: A rule depends on user region, document classification and time of day. Which model fits best?
choices: Plain RBAC with one role per combination
quiz.why: Attribute-based policies express context-dependent rules without role explosion.

lesson.intuition: Authentication is showing your badge at the front door; the company's security desk (the IdP) issues the badge. Authorization is which rooms the badge opens. OAuth is a valet key: it lets an app or agent drive your car to one place without handing over your house keys. Agents should always carry the user's valet key, never a master key.
how: Delegate login to the customer's IdP via SAML or OIDC; verify every assertion or token.
Provision and deprovision users with SCIM.
Map IdP groups to roles (RBAC); add ABAC policies where context matters.
Issue short-lived, scoped, audience-bound tokens.
Give agents delegated tokens and enforce authorization in APIs and retrieval.
lesson.example: An HR assistant serves 8,000 employees. Login uses OIDC with Entra ID, and the 'HR-Partners' group maps to the hr_partner role. An ABAC rule allows reading a salary record only if user.role = hr_partner and user.region = record.region. When an HR partner in the EU asks the agent about salaries, the search tool runs with her token, filters by region and returns only EU records. A US partner asking the same question gets zero EU rows, without relying on the prompt at all.
mistakes: Agents using a shared service account with admin rights.
Putting access rules in the system prompt instead of in code.
Skipping signature, audience or expiry checks on tokens or SAML assertions.
No SCIM deprovisioning, so people who leave keep access.
lesson.enterprise: A legal-tech vendor wins a deal only after adding SAML SSO, SCIM deprovisioning and document-level ABAC. In the security review, the customer's CISO tests that a contractor account removed in Okta loses access within minutes and that the agent cannot retrieve matters outside the contractor's practice group.
takeaways: Delegate authentication to the customer's IdP via SAML or OIDC.
Verify signature, issuer, audience and expiry every time.
RBAC for coarse access, ABAC or ReBAC for context and data-level rules.
Agents act with the user's down-scoped token; enforce authorization outside the prompt.
lesson.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant App as App / Agent
  participant IdP as IdP (Okta / Entra)
  participant API as Tool API
  U->>App: Open app
  App->>IdP: OIDC auth request (PKCE)
  IdP-->>App: ID token + access token (scoped)
  App->>API: Tool call with user token
  API->>API: Verify token, RBAC + ABAC check
  API-->>App: Only permitted data
lesson.diagramAlt: Sequence diagram: the user opens the app, the app redirects to the IdP with an OIDC request using PKCE, the IdP returns an ID token and a scoped access token, and the app or agent calls a tool API with the user's token. The API verifies the token and applies RBAC and ABAC checks, then returns only permitted data.

subjects.title: Caching, Queues and Background Jobs
subjects.why: LLM calls are slow and expensive, and ingestion and agent runs take minutes. Caches and queues keep the product responsive and the bill predictable.
subjects.explainer:
Three patterns carry most AI back ends. Caching stores results you'll need again: exact-match response caches, embedding caches keyed by content hash, and provider prompt caching for long shared prefixes. Queues decouple producers from consumers so a spike of uploads or agent tasks doesn't overload workers or the model API. Background jobs run slow work (ingestion, long agent runs, report generation) outside the request, with status the user can poll or be notified about.

The hard parts are invalidation, retries without duplicates, dead-letter handling and visibility into backlog.

resources.title: Redis documentation: Develop with Redis
resources.why: Redis data types, commands, client libraries and patterns for caching, queues (lists, streams) and rate limiting, with an interactive command tutorial.

resources.title: Celery: Introduction
resources.why: What a task queue is, how Celery distributes tasks to workers via a broker such as Redis or RabbitMQ, and its retry and scheduling features.

resources.title: Amazon SQS: dead-letter queues
resources.why: How SQS moves messages that repeatedly fail into a dead-letter queue (maxReceiveCount, retention, redrive) so they can be debugged without blocking the queue.

resources.title: Anthropic prompt caching docs
resources.why: Cache stable prompt prefixes with cache_control to reduce cost and latency. Covers TTLs, minimum cacheable length and cache write vs read pricing.

resources.title: Slack: Scaling Slack's Job Queue
resources.why: How Slack put Kafka in front of its Redis-based job queue after an outage, while handling over 1.4 billion jobs on peak days at up to 33,000 per second.

subjects.project: Move document ingestion out of the upload request into a queue with workers. Cache embeddings by content hash, add retries with a dead-letter queue, and expose job status to the UI.

topics.title: Caching for AI workloads
topics.explainer: Cache at the layer where work is repeated. Embedding the same chunk twice is pure waste, so key embeddings by a hash of the text and model name. Exact-match response caches (key = hash of model, prompt and parameters) help for repeated queries such as FAQ bots. Provider prompt caching discounts long, stable prefixes such as system prompts and tool definitions. Every cache needs a TTL or an invalidation rule tied to the source data: when a policy document changes, cached answers built from it must expire. Redis is the usual store; measure hit rate, latency saved and cost saved.

subtopics.title: Cache keys
subtopics.text: Include everything that changes the result: model, version, prompt, parameters and tenant.

subtopics.title: Embedding cache by content hash
subtopics.text: Never re-embed identical text; key by sha256(text) plus the embedding model.

subtopics.title: TTL and invalidation
subtopics.text: Expire on time and on source change; stale answers are a correctness bug.

subtopics.title: Measuring value
subtopics.text: Track hit rate, p95 latency and dollars saved per cache.

topics.title: Queues, workers and background jobs
topics.explainer: A queue (Redis, SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) holds work items; workers pull and process them at a controlled rate. This absorbs spikes, enforces concurrency limits towards rate-limited model APIs, and lets you scale workers independently. Delivery is usually at-least-once, so handlers must be idempotent. Failed messages are retried with backoff and, after N attempts, moved to a dead-letter queue for inspection. Long-running jobs need status records (queued, running, succeeded, failed) and progress reporting. Watch queue depth and age of the oldest message as primary health signals.

subtopics.title: At-least-once delivery
subtopics.text: Expect duplicates; make handlers idempotent with keys or upserts.

subtopics.title: Concurrency and rate control
subtopics.text: Size the worker pool to stay inside model API rate limits.

subtopics.title: Retries and dead-letter queues
subtopics.text: Retry with backoff, then park poison messages in a DLQ with the error.

subtopics.title: Job status and observability
subtopics.text: Persist job state, show progress, and alert on queue depth and oldest-message age.

quiz.q: Users upload 500-page PDFs and the upload request times out. Fix?
choices: Enqueue ingestion as a background job and return a job ID
Raise the HTTP timeout to 30 minutes
Ask users to upload smaller files
quiz.why: Slow work belongs in background workers with status polling or notifications.

quiz.q: Your queue delivers at least once. What must handlers be?
quiz.why: Duplicates will happen; processing twice must not cause double effects.

quiz.q: What should an embedding cache key include?
choices: Hash of the text and the embedding model and version
quiz.why: Same text with a different model gives different vectors.

lesson.intuition: A cache is a sticky note with yesterday's answer: fast, but you must throw it away when the facts change. A queue is a ticket dispenser at a busy counter: customers take a number, workers serve them at a steady pace, and nobody gets turned away just because ten people arrived at once.
how: Find repeated work (same embeddings, same prompts, same prefixes) and cache it with correct keys and TTLs.
Move anything slower than a couple of seconds into background jobs.
Put a queue between producers and workers and size workers to downstream rate limits.
Make handlers idempotent; retry with backoff and dead-letter poison messages.
Expose job status and monitor queue depth, age and DLQ size.
lesson.example: A knowledge base re-indexes nightly: 1.2M chunks, of which 96% are unchanged. Embedding everything costs 1.2M × 500 tokens = 600M tokens, about $12 at $0.02/M, and takes 3 hours. A content-hash cache embeds only the 48,000 changed chunks (24M tokens, about $0.48) in 8 minutes. Ingestion jobs run through a queue with 16 workers, capped at the embedding API's 3,000 requests per minute.
mistakes: Cache keys that omit the model version or tenant.
No invalidation, so answers outlive the policy that produced them.
Non-idempotent handlers on an at-least-once queue.
Infinite retries with no dead-letter queue, which blocks the queue.
lesson.enterprise: An insurer's claims assistant generates a summary for every new claim document. Running the summaries as queued background jobs, capped at the provider's rate limit, keeps the claims UI responsive at month-end peaks. A dead-letter queue surfaces the 0.3% of documents that fail OCR for manual handling instead of silently dropping them.
takeaways: Cache repeated work with complete keys and real invalidation.
Slow work goes to background jobs with visible status.
Queues absorb spikes and enforce rate limits.
At-least-once delivery requires idempotent handlers and a DLQ.
lesson.diagram:
flowchart LR
  UP["Upload API"] -->|"enqueue job id"| Q[["Queue"]]
  Q --> W1["Worker"]
  Q --> W2["Worker"]
  W1 --> C{"Embedding cache hit?"}
  W2 --> C
  C -->|"no"| EMB["Embedding API (rate-limited)"]
  C -->|"yes"| IDX[("Index")]
  EMB --> IDX
  W1 -->|"after N failures"| DLQ[["Dead-letter queue"]]
  UP -->|"job status"| UI["UI polls / webhook"]
lesson.diagramAlt: The upload API enqueues a job and returns its ID. Workers pull from the queue, check an embedding cache, call the rate-limited embedding API only on a miss, write to the index, and move repeatedly failing messages to a dead-letter queue. The UI polls job status.

case.title: Scaling Slack's Job Queue (Slack Engineering, 2017)
case.summary: Slack's job queue handles business logic too slow for a web request: every message post, push notification, URL unfurl, reminder and billing calculation. On its busiest days it processes over 1.4 billion jobs, at a peak of 33,000 per second. After database contention slowed job execution and Redis reached its memory limit, causing a significant outage, Slack put Kafka in front of Redis as a durable buffer.
case.lesson: Queues need a durable buffer and back-pressure. When consumers slow down, the queue's own storage must not become the next failure point.

subjects.title: Webhooks and Event-Driven Integration
subjects.why: Agents need to react when something happens in a customer's systems (a ticket is created, a payment fails, a document changes). Webhooks and events are how SaaS tells you.
subjects.explainer:
Polling an API every minute is slow and wasteful. With webhooks, the source system sends an HTTP POST to your endpoint when an event occurs. Event-driven integration generalizes this: events flow through a bus or queue (Kafka, EventBridge, Pub/Sub) to any number of consumers, such as an indexing job, an agent and an audit log.
